source.title_on_document: AI-written admissions essays are widespread but penalized

supplement.where: Appendices A to E, pp. 15-36 of the same PDF
supplement.holds: Appendix A: dataset and pipeline details, plus detector validation and selection in A.2.2-A.2.3 (pp. 19-20; applicant-level Table A1, p. 30, and essay-level Table A2, p. 31, give detection/false-positive rates and standard errors); Appendix B: admissions-officer rating exercise (pp. 20-21); Appendix C: essay-quality calibration and adjusted trends (p. 21; Table A3, p. 32, gives dimension weights and confidence intervals; Fig. A4, p. 27, includes the Voice panel); Appendix D: DML details and residual-variation checks (pp. 22-23; Table A4, p. 33); Appendix E: robustness checks (p. 23; Tables A5-A7, pp. 34-36, report coefficients and standard errors for alternative detectors/thresholds, omission of the changed-prompt essay, and binary treatment).

paper_design_summary: The authors analyze 7,462 applications (2020-2025) to a U.S. public policy master's program. They flag AI-written essays with GPTZero, compare LLM-scored, human-calibrated essay quality before and after the release of ChatGPT, and estimate the admission penalty for AI-flagged essays with double machine learning. In a separate exercise, five admissions officers rated 100 matched essays (50 AI-flagged, 50 human) for AI likelihood and quality; no one was assigned to use AI.

studies.label: Admissions records 2020-2025 (before/after ChatGPT; AI-flagged vs non-flagged applicants)

assignment.what_was_assigned: No generative-AI assistance was assigned; the study observes submitted applications across cohorts and detected AI-use levels.
assignment.quote: Because we cannot observe true AI authorship in the application data, our empirical approach depends on the accuracy of AI detection tools, as we use their detection to serve as a proxy for true AI usage.
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration stated in the full text or Appendices A-E; p. 20, Appendix B reports IRB approval only.

arms.name: No assigned AI-assistance arm
arms.description: No intervention arms were assigned; observed comparisons are described under outcomes.

participants.exclusions: Admission outcomes for the 2025 cycle are not analyzed because the program changed its admissions process after seeing preliminary results (p. 6, fn. 4; p. 18, A.1.4). The paper does not print the number of applicants in the 2023-2024 admission models.
participants.who: Corpus of 7,462 applications (five essays each) to a competitive U.S. public policy master's program, six cycles 2020-2025, domestic and international applicants. The paper counts applications, not distinct people.
participants.country: United States (program); domestic and international applicants
participants.quote: we assemble a novel dataset of 7,462 applications to a competitive U.S. public policy master's program submitted across six admissions cycles between 2020 and 2025

ai_tool.name_model: Not observed. Applicants' own generative-AI use, timed by the ChatGPT release (Nov 30, 2022) and detected with GPTZero 3.9 (main) and Pangram 3.1 (robustness)
ai_tool.how_used: Applicants' unobserved, prohibited use of AI assistants. An essay counts as AI-written if GPTZero labels it 'AI' with high confidence (primarily AI-generated).

task.description: Graduate admissions essays (five essays of 250-500 words on motivation, background, public service), scored for quality, not creativity

outcomes.name: Overall essay quality (human-calibrated composite of seven LLM-scored dimensions), by application year
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: gpt-5-mini grades seven rubric dimensions (grammar, style, clarity, prompt responsiveness, voice and originality, public service, leadership) on 5-point scales; weights come from a regression of admissions officers' ratings on the dimensions (Table A3); averaged to the applicant level; in 2020 SD units. Also split into mechanical and substantive quality. Fig. A4 repeats the trends with applicant controls.

contrasts.reported: Figure only, no numbers printed. Text: 'Figure 3 shows a sharp improvement in the overall quality of essays (blue line) after the introduction of ChatGPT, particularly for international applicants'; gains mostly mechanical, 'more modest' on substantive dimensions.
contrasts.locator: pp. 5-6, Section 3.2, Fig. 3; p. 21, Appendix C.2; p. 27, Fig. A4

outcomes.name: Voice and originality dimension of essay quality, by application year, adjusted for applicant covariates
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: One of seven gpt-5-mini rubric dimensions, described as 'voice and originality' (p. 18) and labeled 'Voice' in Fig. A4. Year coefficients relative to 2020 from OLS with applicant controls, in 2020 within-group SD units, SEs clustered at the applicant level. The paper does not say whether rows are essays or applicants.

contrasts.reported: Figure only, no numbers printed; the text does not discuss voice separately. In the Fig. A4 Voice panel, international applicants are near zero in 2023, above zero in 2024, and highest in 2025; domestic applicants are below zero in 2023-2024 and above zero in 2025. These are qualitative readings of the plotted points relative to the 2020 baseline, not numerical estimates.
contrasts.locator: p. 27, Fig. A4 ('Voice' panel); p. 18, A.1.2 (definition)

outcomes.name: Admission (binary) per AI-flagged essay, 2023-2024 cycles
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Admission decision regressed on the count of an applicant's GPTZero-flagged essays. Unadjusted OLS (linear probability), DML partially linear model with about 400 applicant covariates, and DML that also controls for the 14 essay-quality measures. Robustness: Pangram (Table A5), looser thresholds and exclusion of the changed-prompt essay (Table A6), binary any-AI treatment (Table A7).

contrasts.treatment_arm: Each additional essay flagged as AI-written
contrasts.control_arm: Applicants with fewer or no AI-flagged essays (non-random, covariate-adjusted)
contrasts.reported: AI Count: OLS -0.077*** (0.007); DML -0.015** (0.006); DML + essay quality -0.026*** (0.006). AI Count (2023): -0.081*** (0.013), -0.015 (0.012), -0.021 (0.013). AI Count (2024): -0.076*** (0.008), -0.013* (0.006), -0.021** (0.007). Text: AI users submitted 2.32 AI-written essays on average, 'an aggregate 3.48 p.p. decrease'; 'about 6.0 p.p.' with essay-quality controls.

studies.label: Admissions-officer rating exercise (AI detection and essay quality)

assignment.what_was_assigned: No generative-AI assistance was assigned; existing matched essays were presented to officers in random order for ratings.
assignment.quote: Each officer was tasked to review all 100 essays sequentially, in a random order, with the option to pause and resume their reviews at any time.
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration stated in the full text or Appendices A-E; p. 20, Appendix B reports IRB approval only.

arms.name: No assigned AI-assistance arm
arms.description: No intervention arms were assigned; observed comparisons are described under outcomes.

participants.exclusions: Rater 1 rated 60 of the 100 essays; the other four rated all 100 (460 ratings). For the quality-weight model, 22 ratings of 'very likely AI' were dropped (p. 21).
participants.who: Five admissions staff members at the partner program. They rated 100 essays from 2023-2024 (50 GPTZero-flagged AI, 50 human), matched 1:1 on applicant characteristics, shown in random order.
participants.quote: we recruited five staff members who were going to review applications in the upcoming admissions cycle (2025–2026 cycle). We selected 100 essays (50 human, 50 AI) submitted in either 2023 or 2024

ai_tool.name_model: None used by the raters; essays labeled AI by GPTZero
ai_tool.how_used: Raters judged essays that applicants had written with or without AI. The raters had no AI assistance.

task.description: Rate each admissions essay on a six-point AI-likelihood scale and a six-point quality scale relative to a typical essay

outcomes.name: Admissions officers' quality rating of AI-flagged vs human essays, and its relation to perceived AI likelihood
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Six-point quality rating ('Much weaker' to 'Much stronger'), regressed on AI likelihood, LLM-based quality and GPTZero AI-written indicator, with reviewer fixed effects; SEs clustered by applicant. Detection: AUC 0.70 (95% CI [0.65, 0.75]) (p. 8).

company_involvement.description: GPTZero provided in-kind support through free API access. Its commercial detector supplies the AI-authorship labels used in the main analyses; the paper also cites GPTZero's own technical report [22] when discussing detector error rates.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1, Acknowledgments; p. 3, Section 3.1; p. 12, reference [22]

eligibility.reason: No people were randomly assigned to generative-AI assistance: S1 observes admissions submissions across time and detected AI use (pp. 2-3, Sections 2-3; p. 18, A.2), while S2 randomizes only the presentation order of existing essays (p. 20, Appendix B), so criterion 1 is not met and core remains no. The 7,462 observations are applications, with no distinct-person analysis count reported, so criterion 2 remains unclear (p. 2, Section 2; p. 15, A.1). Criterion 3 is met by the LLM-scored 'voice and originality' dimension of the submitted essays (p. 18, A.1.2; p. 27, Fig. A4, Voice panel), an output-level originality measure under the codebook's novelty definition. This supports observational context, although voice and originality are combined and no separate originality rubric or numerical year coefficients are printed. The five-officer perception exercise does not independently qualify for the core or context evidence under codebook Section 3 (p. 20, Appendix B).

one_line_finding: In a corpus of 7,462 applications (2020-2025) to a U.S. public policy master's program (p. 2, Section 2), 56.1% of 2025 applicants submitted at least one GPTZero-flagged AI essay (p. 30, Table A1), LLM-scored essay quality rose after ChatGPT (figure only, pp. 5-6, Fig. 3), and in the 2023-2024 cycles each additional AI-flagged essay was associated with a 1.5 percentage-point lower admission probability after adjustment for applicant covariates (DML -0.015, SE 0.006; p. 7, Table 1; p. 22, Appendix D).
